question: What are good benchmarks and evaluation strategies for comparing obstacle avoidance strategies in mobile robots?

sections.title: Benchmark Utility and Task Definition
sections.text: Obstacle avoidance is a fundamental task in robotics, defined by the goal of reaching a destination without collision [3]. It serves as a valuable benchmark for testing learning algorithms [2] and was utilized in some of the earliest works involving evaluative adaptation with Genetic Algorithms on real robots, as well as for testing Particle Swarm optimization [2]. The task is particularly suitable for benchmarking because it can be implemented with different numbers of robots and relies on basic sensors and actuators available in most mobile platforms [2]. Furthermore, multiple mobile robot systems offer significant incentives to researchers due to their distributed nature in time and space and their high efficiency [1].

sections.title: Algorithmic Approaches and Planning Types
sections.text: Several algorithms have been proposed for obstacle avoidance, each possessing distinct drawbacks and benefits [3]. Path planning algorithms for mobile robots generally focus on maneuvering from a starting point to a destination while minimizing distance traveled or energy consumed [11]. There are generally two types of motion planning approaches for robots, such as cleaning robots: off-line (static) and on-line (dynamic) planning, categorized by the behavior of obstacles [10]. Global obstacle avoidance requires full knowledge of the static environment to search for the target from an initial location [9]. In contrast, Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) algorithms have been successfully applied to challenging robot motion planning and under-actuated nonlinear control problems [8]. A novel hybrid navigation approach has also been proposed for collision-free movement in dynamic environments [6], and another proposed method combines global path planning with reactive methods to guarantee safe navigation [6].

question: What are existing methods to elicit user intents when an automation encounters ambiguity, especially in failure cases?

sections.title: Mixed-Initiative and Interactive Clarification
sections.text: When automation encounters irresolvable ambiguities, systems should employ mixed-initiative specification to cooperatively engage users rather than failing or guessing [1]. A central challenge is determining when to automate grounding decisions versus requiring explicit user consultation [1]. In database interfaces, systems like MISP and DialSQL use mixed-initiative approaches to ask follow-up questions that clarify intent, such as distinguishing between 'sales amount' and 'number of sales' [2]. These interactive methods help establish 'common ground' between the user and the AI [2]. However, users can become frustrated if the conversation becomes repetitive or fails to address the core error [2]. Multi-stage clarification is essential; without it, systems may provide direct but non-relevant answers or generic fallback messages, both of which degrade user experience. In the context of natural language queries, a 2025 study emphasizes that irresolvable ambiguities in single-shot execution must be handled through this cooperative engagement [1].

sections.title: Automated Disambiguation and Intent Reasoning
sections.text: Alternative approaches aim to resolve ambiguity without explicit user queries. One 2025 method proposes that LLMs, which implicitly commit to one interpretation, should instead generate structured responses enumerating all valid interpretations with corresponding answers. This approach is trained with reinforcement learning using a dual reward system that balances recall on ambiguous inputs and precision on unambiguous ones, eliminating the need for clarification questions. Another 2020 rule-based system generates discriminative questions to disambiguate between two intents without requiring annotated clarification data, a method extensible to multiple intents. Conversely, a 2025 study challenges the necessity of explicit intent modelling by benchmarking Intent-First versus Direct Response Generation paradigms for service assistants. In dialogue, a 2020 reinforcement learning model clarifies ambiguous questions by suggesting refinements, formulating collection partitioning to select labels that distinguish unambiguous intents, and listing these as intent phrases for user confirmation.

sections.title: Programming-by-Demonstration and Continuous Refinement
sections.text: Specifying intents to cover every case can be tedious, and users may not know all potential cases initially [3]. DiLogics, a programming-by-demonstration system utilizing NLP, addresses this by parsing input data and allowing users to refine their intent continuously during automation [3]. By recording user demonstrations for each step, DiLogics generalizes web macros to novel but semantically similar task requirements [3]. The system employs program synthesis techniques to record user actions and their symbolic relationships within the web DOM structure [3]. Users of DiLogics can successfully create automation programs that satisfy diverse input requests for every task [3]. In error handling, 9 out of 10 users edited the input data table to rephrase segmented steps to the appropriate detail, utilizing error repair techniques at every stage [3].

sections.title: Failure Recovery and Robustness in Automation
sections.text: Deep neural networks do not provide an option for maintaining control when unexpected failures are inevitable [6]. In Robotic Process Automation (RPA), a 2023 systematic literature review analyzed implementation studies regarding process selection criteria, utilizing six electronic repositories (IEEE, ACM, SCHOLAR, SpringerLink, Web of Science, Scopus) with search strings combining RPA terms with selection or criteria, considering only English publications [5]. A 2018 study on implementing robust RPA solutions in large organizations focuses on exception handling, work queue, and data management strategies to increase robot robustness against external application interactions and environment instabilities. In human-robot interaction, a 2018 review of 52 studies highlights that robots in unstructured environments are challenged by frequent failures, with little prior research on communicating these failures and their causes. For task automation, the Pumice system implements multi-modal interaction for end-user programmable agents, noting that existing natural language programming systems are inadequate for domain-general tasks [4]. Pumice addresses the issue of end users using unclear or vague concepts, especially in conditionals, by supporting error recovery and backtracking, and allowing users to teach agents new concepts, a capability where existing systems have limited support [4].

question: What are leading approaches for evaluating complex scientific question answering systems in NLP?

sections.title: Foundational Benchmarks and Metrics
sections.text: The evolution of question answering (QA) evaluation has shifted from rudimentary rule-based systems to modern deep learning architectures and large pre-trained models [1] [2] [3] [4]. A key milestone in this progression was the introduction of contextual word embeddings, where ELMo advanced the state of the art for several major NLP benchmarks, including question answering tasks [1] [2] [3] [4]. For commonsense reasoning, the CommonsenseQA dataset was developed to focus on knowledge encoded in ConceptNet [1] [2] [3] [4]. In the domain of complex reasoning, the DROP benchmark provides 9,536 examples and utilizes a few-shot setting with 4 passages, employing an F1 metric for assessment. For chart-based factoid QA, the ChartQA benchmark introduces a relaxed accuracy metric, while multiple other benchmarks such as ChartCheck, Chocolate, ChartLlama, and ChartX have also been established.

sections.title: Scientific-Specific Evaluation Frameworks
sections.text: Evaluating systems on scientific content requires specialized datasets that address the unique complexities of the domain. SciCUEval is a comprehensive dataset designed specifically for evaluating scientific context understanding in large language models (LLMs) [7]. To address the challenges of open-domain QA, the SF-QA framework offers a simple and fair evaluation approach that modularizes the pipeline, thereby making the task more accessible and reproducible [6]. Additionally, a novel "question-to-question" retrieval approach has been introduced for knowledge-based QA, which avoids the generation step to mitigate associated limitations [5]. These resources, along with others like sciverse_ccsbench and sciverse_scirag, form the core corpus for assessing scientific QA capabilities.

sections.title: Controllable Generation and Automated Testing
sections.text: Recent work has focused on controllable text generation, though existing evaluations primarily test LLMs under single-constraint settings, such as adjusting formality [9]. To expand evaluation coverage, researchers have leveraged the strong text generation capabilities of LLMs to automatically generate questions given a specific context and answer [8]. This automated testing approach allows for the creation of diverse QA pairs without manual annotation. However, the reliance on LLMs for generating evaluation data introduces significant risks. Output variability and hallucinations pose serious threats to the reliability of these LLM-generated results [8]. Specifically, hallucinations can lead to generated questions that introduce information not present in the source context or violate the constraints specified in the prompt [8].

sections.title: Human Evaluation and System Reliability
sections.text: Despite the rise of automated metrics, human evaluation remains critical for assessing complex scientific work. Due to the high complexity of the task, evaluators must be experts in the specific domain and topic [10]. To ensure rigor, the evaluation protocol requires that the evaluator has at least 5 years of experience and has published at least 5 papers in the relevant field [10]. This strict qualification standard acknowledges that general NLP proficiency is insufficient for judging the validity of scientific answers. Furthermore, there is a noted disconnect between QA performance and summary quality, suggesting that optimizing for one metric does not guarantee success in the other [1] [2] [3] [4]. Therefore, a robust evaluation strategy must combine automated benchmarks like DROP and ChartQA with rigorous, expert-led human assessment to fully capture system performance [10].

question: What are good practices for detecting AI-generated texts in situations where false positives are extremely expensive?

sections.title: Threshold-Free Architectures and Calibration
sections.text: To minimize false positives, detection systems should avoid reliance on external calibration datasets, which are often unavailable and introduce variability in real-world accuracy [1]. Agent-X employs a threshold-free aggregation strategy that eliminates this dependency, making accuracy a more practical metric than AUROC, which inherently favors threshold-dependent methods and is inadequate for strict FPR control [1]. This multi-agent framework circumvents the calibration issues of single-LLM approaches, where uncalibrated predictions exhibit systematic overconfidence or underconfidence [1]. Specifically, semantic-steering calibration significantly reduces the gap between predicted confidence and true accuracy, resulting in a better-aligned and more reliable confidence distribution [1]. While existing methods rely on large annotated datasets and external threshold tuning, restricting zero-shot effectiveness, Agent-X provides a practical solution for real-world scenarios [1].

snippets: Existing AI-generated text detection methods heavily depend on large annotated datasets and external threshold tuning, restricting interpretability, adaptability, and zero-shot effectiveness.
Our approach provides a practical, threshold-free solution, significantly advancing AI-generated text detection in real-world zero-shot scenarios.

In contrast, our proposed multi-agent framework inherently circumvents these calibration challenges through its confidence-aware, threshold-free aggregation mechanism. Consequently, $AGENT-X$ substantially improves accuracy, interpretability, and real-world applicability.

Existing detection methods (Mitchell et al., 2023a; Bao et al., 2024) frequently rely on metrics like AUROC, which, while theoretically informative, require selecting optimal thresholds based on external, domain-specific calibration datasets.

In contrast, our proposed method uniquely employs a threshold-free aggregation strategy, eliminating dependency on external calibration sets, thereby making Accuracy an inherently more practical and relevant metric for evaluation.

Although AUROC metrics inherently favor threshold-dependent methods and thus are less aligned with our threshold-free design, $AGENT-X$ consistently exhibits strong and competitive performance across all evaluated datasets and language models.
In practical scenarios, such datasets are often unavailable, significantly limiting these methods' applicability and scalability.
This external threshold calibration introduces variability and often leads to inconsistent and suboptimal accuracy performance in real-world applications.
Additionally, an adaptive Mixture-of-Agent router dynamically selects guidelines based on inferred textual characteristics.
Employing less powerful or smaller-scale LLMs could pose challenges in comprehensively understanding the detection guidelines or accurately performing agent-specific tasks.
A meta agent integrates these assessments through confidence-aware aggregation, enabling threshold-free, interpretable classification.

Specifically, we organize detection guidelines into semantic, stylistic, and structural dimensions, each independently evaluated by specialized linguistic agents that provide explicit reasoning and robust calibrated confidence via semantic steering.

The framework consists of three main components: a router agent for adaptive activation of guideline-specific base agents, guideline-specific base agents organized into three stylistic dimensions (semantic, stylistic, and structural), and a meta agent synthesizing these analyses into a final interpretable classification.
White-box methods utilize model-internal metrics such as entropy, likelihood, and log-rank (Gehrmann et al., 2019a; Bao et al., 2024; Tulchinskii et al., 2024).

While Fast-DetectGPT performs strongly in specific scenarios (e.g., XSum, Writing for ChatGPT), it generalizes poorly to biomedical texts (PubMed), highlighting the superior domain adaptability of our threshold-free method.
An optimized zero-shot detector that replaces the perturbation step of DetectGPT with a more efficient sampling step.

Black-box approaches like DetectGPT (Mitchell et al., 2023a), NPR (Su et al., 2023a), and DNA-GPT (Yang et al., 2023) typically involve multiple evaluations or generations, incurring high computational overhead.

sections.title: Interpretability and Human Oversight
sections.text: In high-stakes environments, algorithms must clearly interpret and explain the critical factors leading to classification to prevent false accusations [3]. Agent-X organizes detection guidelines into semantic, stylistic, and structural dimensions, each evaluated by specialized linguistic agents that provide explicit reasoning [1]. A meta agent integrates these assessments via confidence-aware aggregation, enabling interpretable classification [1]. An adaptive Mixture-of-Agent router dynamically selects guidelines based on inferred textual characteristics, though smaller LLMs may struggle to comprehend these guidelines or perform agent-specific tasks [1]. Despite automated capabilities, labeling results should be regarded as reference guidance rather than definitive judgments, with final decisions made under careful human supervision [2]. This approach is particularly relevant as current SOTA detectors often flag minimally polished text as AI and struggle to differentiate degrees of AI involvement.

sections.title: Performance Metrics and Domain Specificity
sections.text: For practical applications, it is essential to evaluate detector effectiveness using the False Positive Rate (FPR) metric, as only low-FPR systems are considered reliable for commercial use [2]. Detection algorithms should also be cost-effective and capable of accurately detecting both long and short texts [3]. Binoculars demonstrates practical significance by achieving over 90% accuracy in detecting ChatGPT-generated English text at an FPR of 0.01%, even without training on ChatGPT data [2]. It also shows superior reliability compared to Ghostbuster on out-of-domain datasets [2]. In Vietnamese contexts, VietBinoculars achieves at least 99% accuracy, F1, and AUC on out-of-domain datasets such as Gemma-3-12B-News and Sailor2-8B-VuTrongPhung [2]. Using a Closest Point threshold, it achieves the highest performance, with prediction failures occurring only for Qwen3-235B-A22B-FW, DeepSeek-V3, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, and GPT-4o [2]. Texts with scores below the TPR@0.06%FPR threshold are highly likely to be AI-generated [2]. However, Vietnamese text typically exhibits lower True Positive Rates at low FPRs compared to well-represented languages like those processed by Falcon-7B [2]. Identified thresholds may not fully capture the statistical characteristics of Vietnamese.

sections.title: Computational Efficiency and Generalization
sections.text: Black-box approaches like DetectGPT, NPR, and DNA-GPT incur high computational overhead due to multiple evaluations or generations [1]. In contrast, Fast-DetectGPT is an optimized zero-shot detector that replaces the perturbation step of DetectGPT with a more efficient sampling step [1]. However, Fast-DetectGPT generalizes poorly to biomedical texts such as those in PubMed, highlighting the superior domain adaptability of threshold-free methods [1]. White-box methods utilize model-internal metrics such as entropy, likelihood, and log-rank [1]. Cross-domain and cross-generator evaluations reveal substantial generalization gaps, as seen in frameworks using 30 linguistic features. Other tools like DoGEN use Domain Gating Ensemble Networks to weight domain expert detectors , while EditLens quantifies the degree of AI editing through binary and ternary classification. A recent survey summarizes SOTA detection methods, including watermarking and statistical analysis, identifying salient factors affecting detectability. Additionally, a dataset of 788,984 AI-written peer reviews from ICLR and NeurIPS over 8 years benchmarks detection in this specific context. VietBinoculars can also serve as a data-cleaning tool to filter AI-generated texts from training datasets [2].
